# INSIGHTS — summarized, verified findings (accumulate across the whole run)

The JOURNAL is your per-iteration diary; THIS file is the distilled, VERIFIED takeaway a future iteration should read instead of re-reading the whole journal or old sessions/traces. Update it whenever you have a genuinely NEW, confirmed finding (an accepted/rejected RESULT counts as confirmation; a guess does not) — not every iteration needs a new entry. Structure each addition as:

    ## <task or mechanism name>
    - What worked (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id):
    - What didn't (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id):
    - Promising but not yet tried:

## The grading contract: `hard_no_recalc` makes a formula unscoreable (measured on the 40 baseline traces)

This run uses `SPREADSHEETBENCH_SCORING=hard` with `SPREADSHEETBENCH_REWARD_RECALC=0`. The grader
reads **stored cell values** and never recalculates. openpyxl writes a formula as `<f>` with **no
`<v>`**, so a formula cell reads back as **empty** and can never match — however correct it is.

- **Confirmed by direct measurement of the baseline (pre-RESULT, from the traces themselves, not a
  guess):** tasks whose solution code writes formulas pass **0 of 13**; tasks that write literals
  pass **18 of 27**. Seven failing tasks (37378, 46897, 53383, 55049, 6698, 7902, 8942) carry
  `test_case_results=[1]` alongside `test_case_results_no_recalc=[0]` — they solved the spreadsheet
  problem and lost only on the stored-value contract.
- **Refuted:** "the instruction wording tells you when a formula is wanted." 3 of 4 sampled
  *passing* tasks also ask for "a formula". Wording is not a discriminator, so the compute-in-Python
  rule must be unconditional.
- **Refuted:** "the `#N/A` cluster is input NaN propagated through." 54144 and 37456 never read a
  value from the input (no `data_only=True` in either trace); the error tokens come from evaluating
  the agent's own defective formula (Excel-365-only `TEXTSPLIT`; a `$A$2` anchor where the header is
  on row 3). The fix is "your logic is wrong", not "don't propagate".
- Awaiting a RESULT for cand_0001 to confirm the prose fix converts these.

## Verification is the second-largest lever, and it was structurally discouraged

- **Measured:** **39 of 40** baseline traces never re-opened the file they wrote. The single trace
  that did (416-15) passed. The agent read `[Code executed successfully with no output]` as success.
- **Mechanism found:** when `task_template.md` is absent the adapter uses its built-in
  `_TASK_TEMPLATE`, which contains *"once that file exists, you are done"*. Creating
  `task_template.md` at all is what suppresses that line. A future iteration that deletes the file
  brings the line back.
- **Corollary, measured:** the freed budget is already there. 46897 resubmitted a byte-identical
  block 28×, 6698 29×, 55049 27× — the wasted rounds exceed an audit's cost tenfold. The missing
  pieces were a stop condition and a defined next action, not turns.
- **Verified constraint on any audit snippet:** 5 of the 18 passing tasks have legitimately blank
  gold cells (382-10 79% — its task *is* to delete values; 395-36 67%; 402-43 65%; 142-12 40%;
  560-12 33% padding). Treating blank as a defect false-alarms on exactly those 5. Blank must be a
  judgement ("is a value expected here?"), never a reflex, and the prose must forbid padding a range
  to look full.
- Also verified: an unbounded audit print floods context (1280 lines on 9569, ~4451 cells on 48921).
  Cap the sample and print an aggregate count.

## Two mechanical facts about this adapter worth not rediscovering

- `spreadsheet_content` is `pandas.read_excel(..., header=0)`: the preview's **column labels are
  Excel row 1**, and preview row `i` is **Excel row `i + 2`**. 59196 read `ws["D1"]` (blank, its
  header is row 2) and wrote `None` everywhere; 227-40's `iloc[13]` landed on Excel row 15,
  producing exactly its observed 12/20.
- `extract_code` takes only the **FIRST** ```python block in a reply; the rest are silently
  discarded. 46897's opening reply had 6 blocks, so its diagnostic `print`s never ran and it
  resolved a genuine ambiguity by speculation.
- `openpyxl.utils.range_boundaries` **rejects a sheet-qualified range** — split on `!` and strip
  quotes before calling it. `openpyxl`'s `ArrayFormula` is neither `str` nor numeric, so a
  `startswith("=")` check misses it while an `isinstance` type check catches it.
- An **empty** `prompt.md` means "no system message"; a **missing** one falls back to
  `_DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT`. The two are not equivalent.
- 402-43 passes while its pandas round trip **silently drops Sheet1** — grading was confined to
  Sheet2. A latent fragility, not a real pass of the whole workbook.

## A pre-filled cell inside `answer_position` does NOT mean "preserve it"

- **What didn't (confirmed by RESULT, cand_0002):** the clause *"a pre-filled cell in
  `answer_position` proves the rule covers its row"* **broke 2768**, whose `'Sheet1'!H2:H18` is
  **fully pre-filled** in the input (`H2=50, H3=20, H4=0…`) under the header `H1='Expected outcome'`
  and whose gold **overwrites every one of them**. The label on the answer column is not a demo block.
- **Measured, same direction:** at least four tasks have pre-filled target cells their gold *changes*
  — 2768 (all 17), 6698 (`G4=6773`), 56563 (`C14='#NUM!'`, the error you are asked to fix), 48620
  (`E6='Yellow'`, the wrong value you are asked to correct). Any "keep what the user filled in" rule
  attacks all four.
- **The distinction that survives:** a pre-filled cell constrains your *interpretation* (if your
  reading yields nothing for a row the user filled, the reading is wrong) but never freezes its own
  final value. Ship the interpretation half; never the preservation half.

## Boundary guidance must name the QUANTITY, not the operator

- **What didn't (confirmed by RESULT, cand_0002):** a general `<` vs `<=` phrase→operator table
  **broke 51-12**, a numeric-threshold task whose passing trace hinges on
  `val_j >= ref_val*1.1 - 1e-9`. Inviting a 31B reader to re-litigate comparison operators in general
  destabilises tasks that had the comparison right.
- **What to ship instead:** name the quantity. "Open at the end of period P" → compare the closed
  date against P's **last** day. Scoped that way the rule reaches **exactly one task** in the 40
  (43436) — verified by scanning all 40 previews for created/closed/open-period wording.
- **Directional proof that needs no gold workbook:** `closed >= first_day_of_P` is strictly more
  permissive than `closed > last_day_of_P`, so the wrong form can *only* inflate a count — which is
  exactly what 43436's scorer reports ("5 cells hold a number HIGHER than expected").

## `MUST-FIX: []` is not the same as correct — the audit is semantics-blind

- **Measured:** 43436 printed `COUNTS: {'ok': 15} / MUST-FIX: [] / BLANK cells: []` and stopped, on
  five wrong numbers. cand_0001's audit validates type / formula / error / blank; it cannot see a
  wrong count, a wrong lookup or an off-by-one window. The type-level lever is now **exhausted** —
  every remaining failure passes it.
- **Measured adoption:** only **11 of 40** traces ever printed `COUNTS:` (12864, 2768, 395-36, 402-43,
  43436, 463-17, 48588, 55049, 7902, 80-42, 9569). The audit is structurally optional in practice.
- **Promising (shipped untested in cand_0003):** require re-deriving **one** value by hand — or
  reproducing a figure the sheet already gives — before a clean audit counts. 43436 had exactly such
  an anchor and ignored it: column H `Open as of today`. Executed check — the correct endpoint rule
  reproduces it (dept A → 1, dept B → 2) and the wrong one does not, so the anchor really does
  discriminate.
- **Related measurement:** every *passing* Cell-Level task that ran the audit has **zero BLANK** cells
  (12864, 2768, 48588, 55049, 9569, 7902). So "near-empty coverage on a Cell-Level task" is a safe
  trigger for "you misread the instruction" — it cannot fire on a passing task. 6 of the 7
  blank-gold tasks are Sheet-Level.

## The audit snippet's scalar test must include date types (verified by execution)

- `isinstance(v, (int, float, bool, str))` classifies `datetime`/`date`/`time` as `FORMULA-OBJECT` on
  openpyxl 3.1.5. Un-fixed it would send the *passing* date-valued tasks (416-15, 80-42, 9726, 59595,
  53647) back to "fix" correct dates.
- **Independent confirmation from the wild:** 80-42's trace hand-patched it — `elif not isinstance(v,
  (int,float,bool,str)) and not hasattr(v, 'year')`. The agent hit the bug and worked around it.
- cand_0002 shipped the `SCALAR` widening and it was **not** among the tasks it broke.

## Round budget is not the constraint; robustness is

- **Measured:** `{max_turns}` = 30, and **31 of 40 tasks finish in exactly 4 rounds** under
  cand_0001's 4-step procedure — the procedure is followed literally, which makes step structure a
  high-fidelity lever but also means an added step is an added obligation on every task.
- **51-12 is the outlier at 10 rounds** (267-18 next at 7). It is the least robust passing task, and
  it is one of the two cand_0002 broke. Prefer folding a new requirement into an existing step over
  adding a step.

## Verification constraint for successors: gold workbooks may be unreachable

- cand_0002 verified its edits by executing them against the benchmark `init`/`golden` workbooks.
  From cand_0003's sandbox those are **not reachable** — `/mnt/data/spreadsheet/<id>/` holds only the
  one unrelated task id and no `*_golden.xlsx` exists on the filesystem.
- Workable substitutes, in descending strength: (a) execute the candidate snippet against a
  **synthetic workbook reproducing the task's structure** (this is how the input-formula erasure and
  the datetime mis-classification were proven); (b) **directional** arguments from the scorer's own
  `feedback` string (e.g. "HIGHER than expected" + a strictly-more-permissive predicate); (c) counting
  the demo block and matching it against the scorer's stated expected-cell count (227-40: 17 = 17).

## The gold workbooks ARE reachable — check this path before using a synthetic twin

Correcting the note above for successors. From cand_0004's sandbox the benchmark data is at
`/vol/home/skillberry/.cache/capevolve-ci/spreadsheetbench-data/spreadsheetbench_verified_400/spreadsheet/<id>/`
holding `1_<id>_init.xlsx` + `1_<id>_golden.xlsx` (also `sample_data_200/` and `all_data_912_v0.1/`).
`/mnt/data/...` — the path the *agent* sees at runtime — is indeed not populated for the proposer,
which is what cand_0003 observed; the mistake is concluding gold is absent. **Always `find` for
`*_golden.xlsx` before falling back.** With gold in hand, "does this rule reproduce the answer" stops
being an argument and becomes a 20-line script, which is what turned cand_0004's diagnosis exact.

## The instruction's own prose is an unused test oracle (~11 of 40 tasks)

These tasks are help-forum posts, so users routinely walk through their own data and **state the
answer** for specific rows: *"fulfil the first line with 100 pcs followed by balance 20 pcs"* — and
golden agrees exactly. Iterations 1-3 mined the *sheet* for evidence (demo blocks, `as of today`
columns, pre-filled rows); nothing mined the *prose* for checkable assertions.

- **Confirmed by reading golden on every passing task whose instruction states a cell value:** the
  stated value already equals golden in all of them — 142-12 (F10/F13→`'Georgia State WH'`), 37378
  (A2→1, A3→2), 48921 (`4000001`→1), 9726 (→2016-06-12). This makes "reproduce every stated value"
  an unusually safe edit: it prints `MATCH` wherever tasks already pass and can only fire where the
  agent is wrong.
- **The discriminator that makes it safe:** a narrated *sentence* whose quantity you can find in the
  real sheet is **binding**; a *retyped mock table* is **illustrative** — take layout from it, numbers
  from the workbook. Verified on 2768: the narrated totals match Sheet2 exactly (1001-A→70,
  1006-B→120) while its pasted table's Order Qty (20) contradicts the real cell (50).
- **Caveat:** many instructions state a *method*, not a value (50768, 59595, 45635 — checked against
  golden). Any edit here must say "write `none` rather than invent one", or a weaker reader will
  manufacture an oracle.

## Which cell you hand-check decides whether the check can fail

- **Measured on two tasks across two iterations:** 43436 (cand_0003) and 2768 (cand_0004) both
  printed a clean `MUST-FIX: []` *and* a hand-check that agreed, while holding wrong values. 2768's
  hand-check verified H2/H3 — **both already filled in the input**, so it confirmed a copy, not a
  computation. The 2 wrong cells were blank in the input and late in the range.
- **General rule:** prefer a cell the input left **empty** and as **late** in the range as possible.
  Ordering, running-total and allocation bugs leave the early rows correct by construction, so
  checking row 1 is the one check guaranteed not to fail.
- **Necessary carve-out, measured:** **6 of 40 target ranges are fully pre-filled** (267-18, 416-15,
  48620, 55049, 56563, 9726), so "pick an empty cell" is impossible there. Phrase it as *prefer* with
  an explicit fallback, or the rule strands a sixth of the split.

## Sorting is rare in this benchmark, which makes sort rules exceptionally safe to add

Grepping every assistant message across all 40 traces for `.sort(`/`sorted(`/`sort_values`/`rank(`/
`argsort`/`nlargest`/`nsmallest`: **exactly one task's code sorts** (2768). Likewise **exactly one
trace ever hit a `TypeError`**. A rule conditioned on "if you sort" or "if a comparison raises" has a
blast radius of literally one task on this split — worth remembering when the headroom is a single
task and any regression zeroes the candidate.

## The failure mode to watch: an invented sort tie-breaker

2768's 2 wrong cells came from sorting `(issued, req_date, line)` where the instruction named only
"earliest issued date". Rows tying on the named key got re-ranked by the extra keys, and in a running
allocation every later row then drew the wrong amount — while the early rows stayed correct, which is
why the audit looked clean. `sorted()` is **stable**, so ties already keep sheet order (the order the
user reads down the page): the correct tie-break is the one you do not supply. Compounding trap: the
extra key was a mixed date/text column, so the sort raised `TypeError`, and the agent "fixed" it with
a `datetime.max` sentinel — which does not unblock the sort so much as silently move those rows to the
end, changing the very ranking under test. 9 of 40 inputs have such a column.
